title: The uncut self
hookLine: weapons can't cut the self, fire can't burn it

cards: An old photograph: a small child on a beach, squinting into the sun. Nearly everything has changed since: the face, the voice, the opinions, the fears.
And yet the grown-up holding the photo points at the child and says: that's me. What is the me that carries across? Arjuna's grief on the chariot is about bodies: the people he loves will die.
Krishna's answer, early in the second chapter of the Gita, turns to something he says no blade can reach.

teach.b: First, the claim. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self, the one who lives in the body, is never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is killed.

As a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, Krishna says, so the embodied self leaves worn-out bodies and takes up new ones. The body changes the way clothes do; the wearer goes on. Third, four forces.
Weapons do not cut it. Fire does not burn it. Water does not wet it.

teach.h: NOT CUT, BURNED, WET OR DRIED.
teach.b: Wind does not dry it. Four things that can wreck a body, and none of them reaches it. The next verse gives today's word: acchedya.
Uncuttable. Steady, unmoving, ancient, the text says. Fourth, how Hindus hold it.
The self here is the atman, and Hindu schools understand it differently. Some teach that the self, at its depth, is one with the ultimate reality, Brahman.
Others teach that each self is eternal and distinct, and belongs to God in love.
They share this verse. And the setting is hard to forget: Krishna says this on a battlefield, to a man about to fight his own family, and some readers wrestle with that.
Others, in their suffering, find in the verse a place to stand. The pain is real, and it comes and goes. Beneath it, Krishna says, is what was never cut.

how: These verses of the Gita's second chapter are recited, and some families read them at funerals and memorials as a teaching about the self that does not die.

o: unending: the cycle of rebirth that never stops
uncuttable: the self no weapon, fire or water can reach
unbreakable: a warrior's armor blessed by the gods

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna says the self dies when the body is killed
he says it is never born, never dies, and is not killed when the body is killed.
the verse names weapons, fire, water and wind
none of them can cut, burn, wet or dry the self.
all Hindu schools describe the atman in exactly the same way
some teach it is one with Brahman; others that each self is eternal and distinct, belonging to God.

games.q: you're Krishna. Arjuna grieves because the people he loves will die. which picture do you give him for the body?
o: worn-out clothes, set aside for new ones.
games.why: Krishna says the self leaves worn-out bodies as a person throws off worn-out clothes.

practice: Watch what's changing, the breath rising and falling, a sound in the room, a thought passing, and let each one come and go. Then gently turn toward whatever is noticing all of it: the sounds change, but does the hearing?
If something feels steady while everything else moves, rest there, without trying to name it or grab it.

wordCard.voice: Acchedya, the Gita's word for the self weapons cannot cut, fire cannot burn, water cannot wet, wind cannot dry. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Gita 2.24: uncuttable, said of the self.

carryVoice: Your line: uncut. Beneath what comes and goes, Krishna points to what stays. Day seven hundred twenty-six.
